<h1>Federated Learning in Medical AI:<br>When Data Cannot Move</h1>

<p class="subtitle">How it works, when it helps, and what can still go wrong</p>

<p class="presenter"><strong>Geng Sun</strong><br>Industrial PhD · Cercare Medical / Aarhus University<br>18 August 2026</p>

<p class="thesis">Federation does not replace multicentre science.<br>It is one way to make multicentre science possible when data cannot move.</p>
:::

<img src="assets/mri/brain_mri_glioma_00.jpg" class="mri-hero" alt="Public false-color glioma brain MRI used as a restrained teaching visual">

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.1 minutes.

Thesis: The course is about medical collaboration under constraints, not about selling an algorithm.

Opening sentence: "Federated learning becomes interesting at exactly the point where the clinical question is multicentre but the data cannot become multicentre in the usual way."

Main evidence: The title and affiliations frame the applied research context; the public MRI is a visual anchor only.

Clinical translation: Tell the audience that every lesson can be borrowed even if they never run FL.

Transition: Move from the title to a concrete four-hospital dilemma.

Optional skip: Skip image attribution aloud unless asked; keep the limitation visible.

Interaction instructions: Ask for a show of hands: who has worked with data that could not leave its institution?

Exact citation reminders: Public MRI attribution is recorded in `assets/mri/README.md` and `research/image-licence-log.md`.
:::

Timing: 1.4 minutes.

Thesis: The hard part is choosing the collaboration design before choosing the algorithm.

Opening sentence: "Imagine four hospitals that agree on the clinical question but disagree, for legitimate reasons, on what can leave the building."

Main evidence: Use the fictional hospital constraints as a teaching case; do not imply these are real AU or Cercare projects.

Clinical translation: This mirrors grant planning, ethics applications, data-processing agreements, and cohort definitions.

Transition: Introduce the menu of five collaboration designs.

Optional skip: If short on time, read only the question band.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience to silently pick the first design they would propose.

Exact citation reminders: No citation needed; this is an original fictional scenario.

# 2. Five Collaboration Designs {#five-collaboration-designs}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.editorial-two-col .visual-led}
::: {}
![](assets/diagrams/workflows.svg){.visual .tall fig-alt="Five collaboration designs: central data pooling, local-only modelling, federated learning, federated evaluation, and federated analytics."}
:::
::: {}
<div class="design-list compact">
<p><strong>Pool data:</strong> strongest control, highest movement burden.</p>
<p><strong>Stay local:</strong> easiest governance, weakest generalization.</p>
<p><strong>Federate training:</strong> share updates, not raw records.</p>
<p><strong>Federate evaluation:</strong> test where data live.</p>
<p><strong>Federate analytics:</strong> estimate before modelling.</p>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.5 minutes.

Thesis: FL is one design in a larger design space.

Opening sentence: "The first mistake is to make federated learning the answer before the collaboration question has been specified."

Main evidence: Rieke et al. and Kairouz et al. provide broad FL framing; MedPerf and federated analytics separate training from evaluation and analysis.

Clinical translation: A PhD protocol should justify why model updates need to move, not merely say that raw data stay local.

Transition: The menu tells us the options; now zoom in on the one option this lesson is mainly about and ask what actually moves.

Optional skip: Skip local-only detail if the audience already knows the menu.

Interaction instructions: Ask which design they picked on the previous slide; compare with this menu. Emphasize that the cards are not buttons here, but a decision vocabulary: changing the design changes whether the unit of movement is raw data, local models, model updates, test results, or only aggregate statistics.

Exact citation reminders: Rieke et al. 2020; Kairouz et al. 2021; Karargyris et al. 2023.
:::

# 3. One Federated-Learning Round {#one-federated-learning-round}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .round-lab}
::: {.round-panel}
![](assets/diagrams/fl-round.svg){.visual fig-alt="A federated-learning round with local training, update transfer, aggregation, and return of the shared model."}
<p class="callout">Raw patient data stay local. Information still moves.</p>
:::
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame" src="labs/aggregation/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive aggregation sandbox" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/aggregation/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2.0 minutes.

Thesis: Aggregation is an assumption, not a neutral accounting step.

Opening sentence: "One round looks simple: train locally, send an update, aggregate, repeat. The trouble is hidden inside the word aggregate."

Main evidence: FedAvg is the baseline idea, but site size, label quality, prevalence, and fairness goals can point in different directions.

Clinical translation: If a small hospital serves the population you most care about, sample-size weighting can make it nearly silent.

Transition: Step from the mechanism to the state of medical FL evidence.

Optional skip: If the lab fails, describe the three buttons: sample-size, equal site, quality-aware.

Interaction instructions: Use the right-hand sandbox slowly. Click **Sample-size** to show that the largest cohort dominates the aggregate update; click **Equal site** to show that smaller hospitals gain voice but the estimate may become noisier; click **Quality-aware** to include the quality signal. Tick **include quality signal** to let the quality field influence weights; tick **upweight under-represented prevalence** to make the rare-prevalence site more visible. Point to the left bars as site weights and the right bars as local update values; when a control changes, the aggregate update and "largest site weight" readouts change.

Exact citation reminders: McMahan et al. 2017; Kairouz et al. 2021.
:::

## Backup: FedAvg Formula

<div class="backup">

FedAvg updates a shared model by a weighted average of local model parameters or updates:

$$
w_{t+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{n_k}{\sum_j n_j} w_{t+1}^{(k)}
$$

Where \(n_k\) is the number of local training examples at site \(k\). The formula is easy to teach; the clinical policy embedded in the weights is not.

</div>

:::

Evaluate FL like clinical infrastructure, not like a demo.

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.8 minutes.

Thesis: Medical FL has impressive research volume but limited clinically mature evidence.

Opening sentence: "If you search the literature, FL looks huge. If you ask how much of it is real-life clinical use, the picture is much smaller."

Main evidence: Teo et al. reviewed 612 healthcare FL articles from 24,060 records; 32 of 612, or 5.2 percent, were real-life FL applications. Li et al. 2025 and Bujotzek et al. 2025 emphasize implementation hurdles.

Clinical translation: A clinical PhD should separate technical feasibility, external validation, and routine clinical value.

Transition: Use brain cancer as the strongest example where scale and evaluation both matter.

Optional skip: Skip the 64-region metric if time is tight.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience what kind of evidence would change their local practice.

Exact citation reminders: Teo et al. 2024; Li et al. 2025; Bujotzek et al. 2025.
:::

# 5. Brain Cancer: Scale, Benchmarking, Evaluation {#brain-cancer-scale-benchmarking-evaluation}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.brain-grid .visual-led}
::: {.mri-card}
<img src="assets/mri/brain_mri_glioma_00.jpg" alt="Public false-color glioma MRI from Wikimedia Commons">
<p class="source-note">Public teaching visual only; not Pati/FeTS data.</p>
:::
::: {}
<div class="research-progression">
<p><span>1</span><strong>Distributed training</strong><br>71 sites · six continents · 6,314 glioblastoma patients</p>
<p><span>2</span><strong>Distributed benchmarking</strong><br>MedPerf evaluates models without moving test data</p>
<p><span>3</span><strong>Federated external evaluation</strong><br>FeTS: 41 models across 32 institutions</p>
<p><span>4</span><strong>Site-specific failures</strong><br>good average performance can hide weak sites</p>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2.1 minutes.

Thesis: The brain-cancer story moved from large-scale training to distributed benchmarking and then to site-level failure analysis.

Opening sentence: "Brain tumor segmentation is one of the clearest medical examples because the clinical question is rare, imaging-heavy, and multicentre by necessity."

Main evidence: Pati et al. used 71 geographically distinct sites across six continents and 6,314 glioblastoma patients. FeTS 2025 evaluated 41 models across 32 institutions on six continents and showed that average performance can hide institutional and outlier weaknesses.

Clinical translation: Rare-disease AI needs both more sites and more honest reporting of which sites fail.

Transition: Name the first transferable lesson: heterogeneity is signal.

Optional skip: If short, keep the four-step timeline and omit MedPerf detail.

Interaction instructions: Ask why a rare-cancer federation is not automatically a deployable clinical product.

Exact citation reminders: Pati et al. 2022; Karargyris et al. 2023; Zenk et al. 2025.
:::

# 6. Lesson 1: Treat Heterogeneity as Signal {#lesson-1-treat-heterogeneity-as-signal}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.shift-taxonomy}
::: {.shift-card}
<div class="shift-glyph feature"></div>
<strong>Feature shift</strong>
<p>population · scanner · assay · workflow</p>
:::
::: {.shift-card}
<div class="shift-glyph label"></div>
<strong>Label shift</strong>
<p>prevalence and event frequency differ</p>
:::
::: {.shift-card}
<div class="shift-glyph concept"></div>
<strong>Concept shift</strong>
<p>the outcome means something different</p>
:::
::: {.shift-card}
<div class="shift-glyph workflow"></div>
<strong>Workflow shift</strong>
<p>referral, annotation, and treatment pathways change</p>
:::
::::

::: {.center-statement}
Institution is a latent variable. FL makes that fact harder to ignore.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.5 minutes.

Thesis: Heterogeneity is not a nuisance term to average away; it is a clinical clue.

Opening sentence: "When hospitals disagree statistically, the first question is not how to smooth them together. It is what the disagreement is telling us."

Main evidence: Zech et al. showed site-level generalization failures in chest radiograph models; FedBN and related work target feature shift by keeping selected normalization local.

Clinical translation: The same habit applies to any multicentre study: stratify, visualize, and document why sites differ.

Transition: Heterogeneity sounds abstract on a taxonomy slide; the next lab makes one common kind of shift visible on the same MRI image.

Optional skip: Skip method names if the audience is clinically mixed.

Interaction instructions: Ask which of the four shifts they most often see in their own projects.

Exact citation reminders: Zech et al. 2018; Li et al. 2021 FedBN.
:::

# 7. Interactive MRI Domain-Shift Lab {#interactive-mri-domain-shift-lab}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

<div class="lab-slide">
<iframe class="lab-frame full" src="labs/mri-domain-shift/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive MRI domain-shift lab" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/mri-domain-shift/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
</div>

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.9 minutes.

Thesis: Domain shift can be visually obvious, but the evaluation consequence is statistical and clinical.

Opening sentence: "This is the same public MRI image; only the appearance has been changed in the browser."

Main evidence: The lab uses controlled display transformations for intensity, contrast, noise, blur, and bias field, plus illustrative threshold, prevalence, and label-noise controls.

Clinical translation: Before federating, ask whether sites are measuring the same phenomenon in the same way.

Transition: Once sites differ, we need a vocabulary for what should be shared and what should stay local.

Optional skip: Use the reset button and one contrast change only.

Interaction instructions: Move **Intensity** to brighten or darken the image; **Contrast** expands or compresses the tissue separation; **Noise** adds grain; **Blur** reduces edge detail; **Bias field** creates a smooth intensity gradient. Tick **compare baseline split** to split the image against the reset state. In the threshold panel, increasing **Decision threshold** usually lowers apparent positives; **Prevalence shift** changes the simulated positive-rate context; **Label noise** makes the readout less reliable. Say explicitly that these are educational approximations, not scanner physics.

Exact citation reminders: Public MRI provenance in `assets/mri/README.md`; heterogeneity motivation from Zech et al. 2018.
:::

# 8. Shared and Local Models {#shared-and-local-models}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .personalization-lab}
::: {.solution-spectrum}
<div class="spectrum-axis"><span>global</span><span>shared + local</span><span>local</span></div>
<p><strong>Robust global:</strong> harmonize and validate broadly.</p>
<p><strong>Target-aware:</strong> reweight when one institution is the clinical target.</p>
<p><strong>Partial pooling:</strong> shared backbone with local calibration.</p>
<p><strong>Local fine-tune:</strong> useful only when local data are sufficient.</p>
:::
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame" src="labs/personalization/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive shared versus local model lab" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/personalization/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.8 minutes.

Thesis: There is no universal optimum on the shared-local spectrum.

Opening sentence: "Personalization is not a defeat of federation. It is often the honest form of federation."

Main evidence: FedBN keeps normalization local for feature shift; FedWeight reweights patients to mitigate covariate shift in EHR; personalized FL work in multiple sclerosis shows gains can depend on local data sufficiency.

Clinical translation: Shared models need local calibration plans, especially when a hospital is sparse or clinically distinctive.

Transition: The next clinical complication is that sites may not even share the same modalities.

Optional skip: If short, say "partial pooling" and show one slider move.

Interaction instructions: Move **Shared-local mix** toward local-only and shared-only; the curve shows the trade-off between borrowing strength and over-sharing. Increase **Heterogeneity** to widen the gap between mean-site and worst-site performance. Increase **Local data per site** to show when local calibration becomes more plausible. The key readout is not only the mean-site number; point to the worst-site value and the clinical interpretation tile.

Exact citation reminders: Li et al. 2021; Zhu et al. 2025 FedWeight; Pirmani et al. 2025 personalized MS.
:::

# 9. Lesson 2: Missing Modalities Are Design Inputs {#lesson-2-missing-modalities-are-design-inputs}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .missing-lab}
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame" src="labs/missing-modality/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive missing-modality matrix lab" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/missing-modality/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
:::
::: {.method-stack}
<p><strong>Common clinical core:</strong> define what every site can measure.</p>
<p><strong>Modality-specific branches:</strong> aggregate compatible representations only.</p>
<p><strong>Partial aggregation or distillation:</strong> share what can be shared.</p>
<p><strong>Missingness-aware evaluation:</strong> report who lacks what and why.</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.8 minutes.

Thesis: Missing modality is not a nuisance afterthought; it defines what learning problem is possible.

Opening sentence: "A federation may contain MRI, CT, EHR, pathology, and genomics, but no hospital has the full row."

Main evidence: Recent peer-reviewed multimodal FL work and missing-modality methods are emerging; FHBench 2025 and Med-MMFL 2026 are useful benchmarks but must be labelled as preprints.

Clinical translation: The project protocol should say whether missingness reflects workflow, access, disease severity, or random absence.

Transition: Even when raw data stay local, information still moves and privacy needs system-level thinking.

Optional skip: Show the matrix, then read the reconstruction warning.

Interaction instructions: Toggle the modality checkboxes in the matrix. Removing **EHR** or **Pathology** at one hospital changes whether a common-core model is realistic. Sparse rows push the design toward modality-specific branches, partial aggregation, distillation, or missingness-aware evaluation. The audience should see that each tick is not a data-cleaning detail; it changes the feasible scientific question.

Exact citation reminders: Thrasher et al. 2025; Saha et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025 FHBench preprint; Chhetri et al. 2026 Med-MMFL preprint.
:::

# 10. Lesson 3: Privacy is a Systems Property {#lesson-3-privacy-is-a-systems-property}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .privacy-lab}
::: {.privacy-map}
<div class="flow-summary">
<p><strong>Stays local:</strong> raw records, direct identifiers, local preprocessing.</p>
<p><strong>May move:</strong> updates, metrics, counts, logs, released models.</p>
</div>
<p class="callout">"Data stay local" is a starting claim, not a complete privacy argument.</p>
:::
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame" src="labs/privacy-threat-model/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive privacy threat-surface explorer" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/privacy-threat-model/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.7 minutes.

Thesis: Privacy depends on flows, actors, logs, releases, and attack models, not only on where raw data sit.

Opening sentence: "Federated learning changes the privacy problem; it does not delete the privacy problem."

Main evidence: Gradient leakage, membership inference, poisoning, secure aggregation, differential privacy, and governance each address different parts of the threat surface.

Clinical translation: Clinical researchers should ask for a threat model in plain language: who can see what, what could they infer, and who responds if the assumption breaks.

Transition: The same systems thinking applies to evaluation.

Optional skip: Read only the callout and toggle "model released externally."

Interaction instructions: Tick **model updates visible** to show gradients or parameters as an information channel; tick **counts and metrics visible** to expose small-cell and per-site disclosure risk; tick **orchestration logs retained** to add operational metadata; tick **participant can be malicious** to introduce poisoning or inference by a site; tick **model released externally** to add downstream membership and misuse risk. The arrows and prompts change qualitatively; do not turn this into a fake privacy score.

Exact citation reminders: Pati et al. privacy review; Shokri et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2019; Bonawitz et al. 2017.
:::

# 11. Lesson 4: Evaluate the Hospital {#lesson-4-evaluate-the-hospital}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.lab-layout .evaluation-lab}
::: {.eval-protocol}
<p><span>Report</span> global + per-site</p>
<p><span>Stress-test</span> unseen site + temporal drift</p>
<p><span>Calibrate</span> site + subgroup reliability</p>
<p><span>Quantify uncertainty</span> confidence + drift signals</p>
<p><span>Escalate / abstain</span> handoff rules</p>
:::
::: {}
<iframe class="lab-frame" src="labs/evaluation-shift/index.html?embed=1" title="Interactive hospital-level evaluation lab" scrolling="no"></iframe>
<a class="lab-open" href="labs/evaluation-shift/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open full lab</a>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.8 minutes.

Thesis: A clinically acceptable average can still hide an unacceptable hospital.

Opening sentence: "The model that is good on average may be exactly the model that is bad for the hospital you are standing in."

Main evidence: FeTS reports distributed multi-site evaluation; MedPerf formalizes federated benchmarking; recent radiology AI uncertainty work emphasizes postdeployment monitoring and UQ under heterogeneity.

Clinical translation: A study should predefine minimum acceptable performance at the site and subgroup level, not only global AUROC or Dice.

Transition: Now reveal why the algorithm is only the visible top of the federation.

Optional skip: If short, show worst-site and abstention only.

Interaction instructions: Increase **unseen-site shift** to show the weakest hospital falling away from the average. Move the **abstention** control to show how deferring uncertain cases can improve safety at the cost of coverage. If the lab exposes calibration or subgroup controls, use one of them to underline that "good mean performance" is not enough. Ask when the protocol should require local calibration or stop deployment.

Exact citation reminders: Zenk et al. 2025 FeTS; Karargyris et al. 2023; Koutsoubis et al. 2025; TRIPOD+AI.
:::

# 12. The Real-World Federation Stack {#the-real-world-federation-stack}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

::: {.layered-stack}
<div class="model-layer"><strong>Visible top:</strong> model · optimizer · aggregation · schedule</div>
<div><strong>Clinical</strong><span>intended use · population · labels · decision workflow</span></div>
<div><strong>Data</strong><span>harmonization · missingness · provenance · quality control</span></div>
<div><strong>Infrastructure</strong><span>identity · compute · networking · monitoring · incident response</span></div>
<div><strong>Governance</strong><span>ethics · contracts · roles · authorship · withdrawal · maintenance</span></div>
:::

::: {.center-statement .compact}
A federation is a collaboration before it is an algorithm.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.5 minutes.

Thesis: The durable work of FL is mostly clinical, organizational, and infrastructural.

Opening sentence: "The algorithm is what fits on the slide. The federation is what survives contact with real hospitals."

Main evidence: Eden et al. map procedural, relational, and structural governance mechanisms; Li et al. and Bujotzek et al. emphasize real implementation barriers in healthcare and radiology.

Clinical translation: Budget for site coordinators, data stewards, IT, security review, and monitoring, not only GPU time.

Transition: With that stack in mind, map the research frontier for 2026.

Optional skip: Keep only the quote and four below-water groups.

Interaction instructions: Ask which below-water layer usually receives too little budget in their projects.

Exact citation reminders: Eden et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025; Bujotzek et al. 2025.
:::

# 13. Research Frontier Map, 2026 {#research-frontier-map-2026}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.frontier-grid}
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Personalized / target-aware</strong>
Whose hospital should the model serve?<br>
<span>Maturing methods</span> FedWeight.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Multimodal / missing-modality</strong>
What can be shared when rows differ?<br>
<span>Emerging</span> incongruent MMFL.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Foundation models / PEFT</strong>
Can sites adapt large models cheaply?<br>
<span>Promising</span> biomedical FL reviews.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Federated evaluation / analytics / causal</strong>
Do we need training, testing, or estimation?<br>
<span>Practical</span> MedPerf.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Uncertainty, fairness, robustness, drift</strong>
Who is failed by the average?<br>
<span>Essential</span> FeTS + UQ.
:::
::: {.frontier-card}
<strong>Infrastructure, governance, reproducibility</strong>
Who is responsible when it breaks?<br>
<span>Deployment-critical</span> Eden.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2.0 minutes.

Thesis: The frontier is not one topic; it is six coupled research programs.

Opening sentence: "By 2026, the interesting FL questions are less about whether federation can train a model and more about what kind of federation deserves clinical trust."

Main evidence: Personalized, multimodal, foundation-model, federated-evaluation, uncertainty, and governance literatures are all advancing, but not with the same maturity.

Clinical translation: A PhD student can position a project by naming the maturity level of the method, not by presenting every preprint as established.

Transition: The frontier map is broad; now compress it into the few practical habits a clinical researcher can use in the next protocol meeting.

Optional skip: Read one mature area and one emerging area only.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience which frontier fits their current project and whether the evidence is peer-reviewed or preprint.

Exact citation reminders: FedWeight; Thrasher et al.; Li et al. federated foundation models; MedPerf; Eden.
:::

# 14. Practical Takeaways for Clinical AI {#practical-takeaways-for-clinical-ai}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.borrow-grid}
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>1</span>
Write the clinical question and target setting before naming the model.
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>2</span>
Decide what can move: raw data, updates, metrics, models, or only conclusions.
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>3</span>
Treat hospital, scanner, workflow, and label definition as variables.
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>4</span>
Plan for missing modalities and local calibration from day one.
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>5</span>
Evaluate worst-site performance, uncertainty, drift, and abstention.
:::
::: {.borrow-card}
<span>6</span>
Document privacy flows, roles, failure response, and maintenance.
:::
::::

<div class="download-band">
Use the resources page for the full reading path and interactive labs.
</div>

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1.4 minutes.

Thesis: The most useful takeaway is not "use FL"; it is a protocol habit for constrained multicentre clinical AI.

Opening sentence: "So what can a clinical PhD actually use after this lecture? Not a slogan, but a checklist for the next protocol meeting."

Main evidence: The six points come directly from the course: collaboration design, data movement, heterogeneity, missing modalities, evaluation, and governance.

Clinical translation: These are practical questions for grant writing, ethics review, data-processing agreements, analysis plans, and deployment discussions.

Transition: Pause here for questions before the final QR/resource slide.

Optional skip: Read only takeaways 1, 2, and 5.

Interaction instructions: Ask the audience which takeaway would change one of their current projects. Do not open a lab here; this slide is for synthesis and discussion.

Exact citation reminders: TRIPOD+AI; DECIDE-AI; Eden et al.
:::

# 15. Q&A {#qa}

<div class="brand-strip"><img src="assets/brand/au-logo-uk-blue.png" alt="Aarhus University logo"><span class="brand-divider"></span><span class="cercare-brand"><img src="assets/brand/cercare-icon.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true">Cercare Medical</span></div>

:::: {.qa-slide}
::: {.qa-main}
<span>Questions</span>
Bring a clinical AI project; we can map what moves, what stays local, and what evidence would change practice.
:::
::: {.qa-prompts}
<p><strong>Design:</strong> is FL needed, or would federated evaluation / analytics answer the question?</p>
<p><strong>Evidence:</strong> which hospital, subgroup, or drift scenario could fail?</p>
<p><strong>Governance:</strong> who sees updates, metrics, logs, and released models?</p>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2.3 minutes.

Thesis: Questions should be anchored in concrete study design, not abstract FL enthusiasm.

Opening sentence: "I want to leave space for questions, but I will frame them in the same way as the lecture: bring a project, and we can map what moves and what must be evaluated locally."

Main evidence: Use the three prompts to route questions toward design choice, evidence standards, and governance.

Clinical translation: Encourage students to translate their own project into a movement map and an evaluation map.

Transition: After discussion, return to the final QR slide so people can access labs and references.

Optional skip: If there are no questions, ask one seeded question: "When would you choose federated evaluation instead of federated training?"

Interaction instructions: Invite one project-specific question first. If discussion is quiet, ask the room to pick one of the three prompt cards and answer it in relation to their own data.

Exact citation reminders: No new citations; this is a discussion slide.
:::

:::: {.closing-grid}
::: {}
<div class="closing-line">FL helps when the clinical question is shared, but patient-level data cannot or should not be pooled.</div>
<div class="closing-line">It fails when heterogeneity, privacy, evaluation, and governance are treated as afterthoughts.</div>
<div class="closing-line">The transferable habit is to make the collaboration visible.</div>
